title: Can we prove God? (ST I.2)
hook: Thomas thinks reason can reach God's existence, though not everything about God

segments.voice: Yesterday, grace perfects nature: God's gift doesn't flatten what we are, it finishes it. Your line was grace completes. Which of your gifts did you use on purpose? Day one thousand one hundred fifty-five.

Fresh snow, early morning, and a line of small prints crosses the yard, under the fence, and away. Nobody saw the fox. Nobody needs to. The tracks are there, and tracks don't make themselves. You can know that something passed, and even something about its size and its hurry, without ever seeing its face. Now hold that, and ask a big question that Thomas Aquinas asks near the start of the Summa. Can a person, thinking hard and honestly, get to God by reason? Or is God something you can only take on faith? Thomas's answer is neither of the easy ones. Today's word is the question itself.
screen: `PRINTS IN THE SNOW.` → `NOBODY SAW THE FOX.` → `CAN REASON GET TO GOD?`

segments.voice: Thomas takes it in steps. First: is God's existence obvious? In itself, he says, yes, but not to us. And his evidence is a psalm: the fool says in his heart, there is no God. If a person can think the opposite, it isn't obvious to us. Second: can it be shown, then? Yes, Thomas says, but only one way: from effects. We can't start from what God is, because we don't see that. We start from the world, and reason back to its cause, the way you reason from tracks to the fox. For this he leans on Paul, in the Douay-Rheims: "For the invisible things of him, from the creation of the world, are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made." Now the limits, and Thomas is careful about them. Reason can reach that God is. It can't reach everything about God. Later in the Summa he says that God being three persons, Father, Son and Spirit, is known by revelation, not by natural reason. And in the Summa's very first article he says something humbling: even the truths about God that reason can reach would be known only by a few, after a long time, and with many errors mixed in. That's why, he says, God revealed them too. And one more kindness. Thomas says God's existence isn't strictly an article of faith but something faith builds on, the way grace builds on nature. Yet a person who can't follow a proof may simply hold it by faith. No one is shut out for not being a philosopher. So the answer to today's question is yes, and. Reason can reach. It just doesn't reach the end of God.
screen: `OBVIOUS IN ITSELF, NOT TO US.` · `SHOWN FROM EFFECTS, LIKE TRACKS.` · `THAT GOD IS, NOT ALL GOD IS.` · `NO ONE SHUT OUT FOR LACK OF PROOFS.` · then, large: `BEING UNDERSTOOD BY THE THINGS THAT ARE MADE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think carefully. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one question you care about and usually rush past. It might be about God, or about a choice in front of you. Say it to yourself in one plain sentence. Then sort what you have. What do you actually know? What are you only assuming? What would you need to find out? Take each one slowly, and don't decide the answer yet. If your mind wanders, come back to the sentence. If you pray, you can hand the question to God at the end. The bell holds the time.
Can we prove God? Thomas's answer: reason can show that God is, working back from the world, though it can't reach everything about God. Today's word.

Your line: reason can reach. That closes a week that ran from the Our Father's petitions and the final Amen to a boy in a tower, a book that argues fair, and grace that completes. Today, give one hard question five full minutes of careful thought. Day one thousand one hundred fifty-five.

howItsDone: Catholic teaching holds that God's existence can be known by natural reason from created things, and Catholic schools and universities often teach Thomas's arguments alongside the Church's teaching on revelation.

fork.setup: you ask Thomas: can a person get to God by reason, or only by faith? what does he answer?
options: only by faith; reason can't get there.
reason can show that God is, from the world, but not everything about God.
it's obvious to everyone; no reasoning needed.
fork.reveal: Thomas says it isn't obvious to us, but can be shown from effects, leaning on Romans 1:20. Yet the Trinity is known by revelation, and even reason's truths about God would reach only a few without it.

original.note: Latin: a showing from effects back to their cause — the kind of proof Thomas says can reach God.

trapdoor: what you thought: Thomas thought he could prove everything about God.
what it means: reason can reach that God is, working back from the world, but not all that God is.
what a scholar hears: a demonstration quia, from effect to cause; God's existence is a preamble to the articles of faith, not one of them.
recall: a firm habit of doing good
